citation.sourceDocument: Wisconsin DOR 2026 Form 1-ES Instructions, D-101A (R. 1-26) — 2026 Tax Rate Schedules + 2026 Standard Deduction schedules (Wis. Stat. §§71.05(23), 71.06)
citation.sourceNote: Wisconsin's four rates for tax year 2026 — 3.50% / 4.40% / 5.30% / 7.65% (Wis. Stat. §71.06) — are printed in the DOR's 2026 Tax Rate Schedules. Schedule A covers SINGLE AND HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD together (4.40% at $15,110, 5.30% at $51,950, 7.65% at $332,720), so the two statuses share one bracket table; Schedule B is married filing jointly ($20,150 / $69,260 / $443,630). The elevated 5.30% threshold ($51,950 single, up from a purely-indexed ~$29,000) reflects the 2025-27 biennial budget (2025 Wisconsin Act 15, signed 2025-07-03), which widened the 4.40% bracket. Wisconsin's signature feature is its SLIDING standard deduction (§71.05(23)(a)), which the DOR prints as one schedule per filing status. Single: $13,960, reduced by 12% of Wisconsin income over $20,120, reaching $0 at $136,453. Married filing jointly: $25,840, reduced by 19.778% over $29,040, reaching $0 at $159,690. HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD IS A TWO-SEGMENT SCHEDULE and is modeled in full: $18,030, reduced by 22.515% over $20,120 until that curve meets the single line at $58,827, after which it follows the single line ($13,960 less 12% over $20,120) to $0 at $136,453. Because both segments are lines measured from the same threshold, the engine takes whichever gives the larger deduction, which reproduces the printed bands exactly and leaves no crossover figure to drift. On top of the deduction, Wisconsin allows a $700-per-exemption personal exemption — $700 for yourself, $700 for a spouse on a joint return — so $700 single / head of household, $1,400 married jointly. (2025 Act 15 widened the brackets; it did not change the $700 exemption, which the 2026 Form 1-ES worksheet still states.) Married filing separately is not seeded and falls back to the single schedule at launch fidelity; Wisconsin publishes a separate Schedule C and a $12,280/19.778%/$13,779 deduction schedule for it. The $700-per-dependent exemption, the $250 age-65 exemptions, the §71.05(6)(b) retirement-income exclusion (2025 Act 15, age 67+), the married-couple credit, the school-property-tax and other Wisconsin credits, and the WAGI-rounded lookup tables (the engine uses the continuous statutory formula) are omitted at launch fidelity. Wisconsin levies no local income tax. Worked example, single $60,000: deduction = $13,960 − 12%·(60,000 − 20,120) = $9,174.40; taxable = 60,000 − 9,174.40 − 700 = $50,125.60; tax = $528.85 + 4.40%·(50,125.60 − 15,110) = $2,069.54. Worked example, head of household $40,000 (first segment): deduction = $18,030 − 22.515%·19,880 = $13,554.02, which beats the single line's $11,574.40; taxable = $25,745.98; tax = $996.83. The brackets and deduction schedules index annually; the refresh adapter anchors the standard-deduction maxima and the per-status bracket tables roll alongside them as the reviewer's data-only step. Verified line by line against the Wisconsin DOR's 2026 Form 1-ES Instructions (D-101A (R. 1-26), stating the law as of 2026-01-16) on 2026-08-29, cross-checked against Wis. Stat. §§71.05(23)/71.06 and 2025 Wisconsin Act 15.
